# Introduction

This Vignette describes how the `greedy_parsimony()` function can be used to infer proteins from peptide identifications using the Occam's razor principle. The method tries to find a minimal set of proteins which can explain all the peptides identified.

```{r loadData}
library(prozor)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

file <- system.file("extdata/IDResults.txt.gz", package = "prozor")
specMeta <- readr::read_tsv(file)
head(specMeta) |> knitr::kable()
```


Annotate peptide sequences with protein sequences from two fasta files on with reviewed entries only (sp) and the other with reviewed and Trembl entries (sp/tr).

```{r fig.cap = "Number of proteins in the All and Canonical database."}
resAll <- read_peptide_fasta(system.file("p1000_db1_example/Annotation_allSeq.fasta.gz", package = "prozor"))
resCan <- read_peptide_fasta(system.file("p1000_db1_example/Annotation_canSeq.fasta.gz", package = "prozor"))

db_sizes <- data.frame(database = c("All", "Canonical"), proteins = c(length(resAll), length(resCan)))
ggplot(db_sizes, aes(x = database, y = proteins)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0072B2") +
  geom_text(aes(label = proteins), vjust = -0.3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "proteins")
```

```{r}
length(unique(specMeta$peptideSeq))
upeptide <- unique(specMeta$peptideSeq)
annotAll <- annotate_peptides(upeptide, resAll)
head(select(annotAll, !proteinSequence)) |> knitr::kable()

annotCan <- annotate_peptides(upeptide, resCan)
```



```{r fig.cap="Number of peptide protein matches for the All and Canonical database."}
matches <- data.frame(database = c("All", "Canonical"), matches = c(nrow(annotAll), nrow(annotCan)))
ggplot(matches, aes(x = database, y = matches)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0072B2") +
  geom_text(aes(label = matches), vjust = -0.3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "peptide protein matches")
```

We can see that using the larger fasta database reduces the proportion of proteotypic peptides.
A proteotypic peptide is one which matches only a single protein.

```{r proteotypicPetides, fig.cap="Proportion of proteotypic peptides."}
proteotypic <- data.frame(
  database = c("All", "Canonical"),
  percent = c(
    sum(table(annotAll$peptideSeq) == 1) / length(table(annotAll$peptideSeq)) * 100,
    sum(table(annotCan$peptideSeq) == 1) / length(table(annotCan$peptideSeq)) * 100
  )
)
ggplot(proteotypic, aes(x = database, y = percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0072B2") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f %%", percent)), vjust = -0.3) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "% proteotypic peptides")
```


# Protein Inference 


We can now identify a minimal set of proteins explaining all the peptides observed for both databases

```{r}
precursors <- distinct(specMeta, peptideModSeq, precursorCharge, peptideSeq)

# peptide protein matches as points; rows and columns sorted by their number of matches
plot_matches <- function(pepprot) {
  peptide_rank <- rank(-Matrix::rowSums(pepprot > 0), ties.method = "first")
  protein_rank <- rank(-Matrix::colSums(pepprot > 0), ties.method = "first")
  nonzero <- Matrix::summary(pepprot)
  ggplot(data.frame(peptide = peptide_rank[nonzero$i], protein = protein_rank[nonzero$j])) +
    geom_point(aes(x = protein, y = peptide), shape = 15, size = 0.5) +
    scale_y_reverse() +
    labs(x = "proteins, most peptides first", y = "peptides, most proteins first")
}
```

## Protein Inference for database with Trembl identifiers

```{r greedyTrembl, fig.cap="Peptide protein matches for the All database. Rows - peptides, columns - proteins, point - peptide protein match."}
annotatedPrecursors <- inner_join(
  precursors,
  select(annotAll, peptideSeq, proteinID),
  by = join_by(peptideSeq),
  relationship = "many-to-many"
)

xx <- prepare_matrix(annotatedPrecursors, protein_id = "proteinID", peptide_id = "peptideSeq")
plot_matches(xx)
dim(xx)
xx[1:10, 1:100]
xxAll <- greedy_parsimony(xx)
```

## Protein Inference for Reviewed/Canonical database

```{r greedyCanonical, fig.cap="Peptide protein matches for the Canonical database. Rows - peptides, columns - proteins, point - peptide protein match."}
annotatedPrecursors <- inner_join(
  precursors,
  select(annotCan, peptideSeq, proteinID),
  by = join_by(peptideSeq),
  relationship = "many-to-many"
)

xx <- prepare_matrix(annotatedPrecursors, protein_id = "proteinID", peptide_id = "peptideSeq")
plot_matches(xx)
xx[80:100, 1:10]
xxCAN <- greedy_parsimony(xx)
```

# Conclusion

We see that the number of proteins needed to explain all the peptides is practically identical for both databases. Also in practice using a database with more entries does not lead to more identified proteins. On the contrary, it might even reduce the number of proteins identified.

```{r fig.cap="Number of proteins before and after protein inference."}
inference <- data.frame(
  database = rep(c("All", "Canonical"), each = 2),
  stage = factor(rep(c("before", "after"), 2), levels = c("before", "after")),
  proteins = c(
    length(unique(annotAll$proteinID)), length(unique(unlist(xxAll))),
    length(unique(annotCan$proteinID)), length(unique(unlist(xxCAN)))
  )
)
ggplot(inference, aes(x = stage, y = proteins)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0072B2") +
  geom_text(aes(label = proteins), vjust = -0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~database) +
  labs(x = "protein inference", y = "proteins")
```
